title: Hello, Python
summary: A program is a list of instructions Python runs from the top down. print() shows text on the screen; text goes inside quotes. Comments start with #.
objectives: Write and run a program that prints text.
Put text in quotes, and print numbers without them.
Print several lines, and a blank line.
Write a comment that Python skips.

real.text: prints the same board every morning on a slate. Today a program will do it.

slides.say: `print` is a **function**: a named action Python already knows. You call it by writing its name, then round brackets with what to show inside.
points: `print("Hello")` shows **Hello**.
The round brackets are not optional.
Each `print` starts a new line.
p: `print` is a **function**: a named action Python already knows. You call it by writing its name, then round brackets with what to show inside.
`print("Hello")` shows **Hello**.
The round brackets are not optional.
Each `print` starts a new line.

visual.why: Two prints, two lines. The quotes are not shown: they only mark where the text starts and ends.

terms: a named action, like `print`, that you run by writing its name and brackets

slides.say: Text in a program is called a **string**. It goes between quotes, double `"…"` or single `'…'`, as long as both ends match. Numbers don’t need quotes.
points: `print("42")` and `print(42)` both show 42, but one is text and one is a number.
Use double quotes when the text has an apostrophe: `"Ravi's"`.
Without quotes, Python thinks a word is a name it should know.

lecture.title: More lines, and notes to yourself

slides.say: Python runs line 1, then line 2, then line 3. Change the order of the lines and you change the order of what appears.
points: An empty `print()` prints a blank line.
Numbers can be printed and worked out: `print(2 + 3)` shows 5.
Several values in one print are joined with a space.
p: Python runs line 1, then line 2, then line 3. Change the order of the lines and you change the order of what appears.
An empty `print()` prints a blank line.
Numbers can be printed and worked out: `print(2 + 3)` shows 5.
Several values in one print are joined with a space.

slides.say: Anything after a `#` on a line is a **comment**. Python ignores it. Comments are for people: you next week, or a teammate.
points: Put a comment above a tricky line to say **why** it’s there.
A `#` at the start of a line turns the whole line off.
Too many comments are noise: name things well instead.

terms: a note after `#` that Python skips

slides.say: Python is fussy in a useful way: `print` must be spelled exactly, in small letters, with round brackets. When it isn’t, Python stops and tells you which line it couldn’t understand.
points: `Print` and `PRINT` are different names, and Python only knows `print`.
Every `(` needs its `)`.
Every quote needs its partner.

points: A **program** runs from the top down, one line at a time.
`print(...)` shows things; each print starts a new line.
Text goes in matching **quotes**; numbers don’t.
`#` starts a **comment** that Python skips.
⚠ Watch out: `Print` isn’t `print`, and every quote and bracket needs its partner.
recap.cheat: print("text in quotes"); numbers without; # for notes.

cards.back: Shows **Hi** on the screen and moves to a new line.
Text in a program, between matching quotes: `"Hi"` or `'Hi'`.
`#`: Python skips the rest of the line.
Without quotes Python looks for a **name** called Hello. Text needs quotes.
